newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada economy, market outlook bullish-Scotiabank.
newsitem.headline: Canada economy, market outlook bullish-Scotiabank.

text.p: Canada's economy is on track for robust growth this year, but the Bank of Canada will hold off raising rates until at least autumn, Scotia Capital Markets economists predicted on Thursday.
The combination of low rates and strong growth should boost bond and equity markets, economists told a conference.
"Canada is in a very powerful recovery," said Michael Manford, chief economist of Scotia Capital Markets, a unit of Bank of Nova Scotia.
Manford predicted the economy would see real growth of 3.6 percent in 1997 and likely more than 3 percent growth next year.
But with inflation subdued, there was little reason for the Bank of Canada to hike interest rates in the near future, Manford said.

He forecast that the central bank would not hike rates until autumn and he saw 100 basis points of tightening by next spring. Even with interest rates now at their lowest in decades, Manford expected inflation to remain below 2 percent for the rest of the year.
The combination of low interest rates, strong growth and subdued inflation would allow Canadian stocks and bonds to appreciate further this year, Scotia Capital economists said.
"One should still remain fully invested in equities and expect that the equity market can outperform bonds in the next 12 months," Diane Urquhart, head of equity research with Scotia Capital said.
Stocks would be driven by strong profit growth, lower long-term interest rates and the flow of funds into equity markets, Urquart predicted.

She forecast the benchmark Toronto Stock Exchange 300 Index, now at 6500, would reach 7000 in 1997 and 7600 in 1998. The TSE 300 could reach 8000 before the end of the current economic cycle, she said.
Bond investors would do best if they put their money in the long end of the Canadian yield curve, said David Adamo, managing director of fixed-income research for Scotia Capital Markets.
Adamo predicted long bond yields would fall below current levels in the next year.
Canadian long bonds may slightly outperform their U.S. counterparts over the next year, but any gains would be limited, Adamo said.
The spread between the Canadian and U.S. 30-year benchmark bonds fell to zero at one point this week from 200 basis points in October 1995 .
"Spreads have probably tightened as much as they're going to at the long end," Adamo said.
